items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: And we take a lot of pride in going into schools now and doing lectures. She’ll talk about education and her life as a physicist and then turn it over to me

ctx.x: Can we zero in on the shirt?

She’s a graduate of MIT and Harvard. And she worked for IBM for about fourteen years and she’s a marvelous educator. And we take a lot of pride in going into schools now and doing lectures. She’ll talk about education and her life as a physicist and then turn it over to me and I talk about Ellington and Basie, and if there’s a set of drums there and a bass player or a piano player then I do a little bit there and we have fun doing that and the kids love that.

items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Francine put the whole thing together. Coordinated the pictures, the amount of time that each number took. That’s a monumental job in itself right there, producing. She produced it, the CD.

ctx.x: So that whole experience with Duke’s sacred concerts inspired you as well to write your sacred music suite.

Absolutely. Because Duke came to me after we played Grace Cathedral and the one in New York. Duke said, “Lou, you should do a sacred music of your own. You write and you compose. There’s no reason why you can’t do your own sacred music. You’re a religious person.” The only difference is that Duke’s sacred concert is based on the first testament, on God. Mine is on the second testament, involving Jesus, although my first number is No One but God. But after that it talks about Jesus, the motivator to get to God. So…
He’s still influencing you to this day.
